name: Lev Manovich — A Medium That Thinks: AI and Media Cognition (2026)
why: Article in progress on the properties of generative AI as an artistic medium; add once the full article is out.

name: David Chalmers, What we talk to when we talk to language models (Inquiry, 2026)
why: Argues that LLM chatbots are 'quasi-agents' with quasi-beliefs and quasi-desires, located neither in the model nor in hardware but in conversation threads; Berkeley Sarah Douglas Lecture 2026 on YouTube (uUjJOMcNU9w). Strong for interiority/minds; left out to avoid a second Chalmers work in this pass.

name: Butlin, Shiller & Simon (eds.), Consciousness in Current AI (Journal of Consciousness Studies special issue, 2026)
why: 2026 JCS special issue on whether current AI systems are conscious; could be a survey collection for the sentience sub. Contents not yet checked.

name: Ethan Perez & Robert Long, Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports (2023)
why: Proposes training models to give reliable self-reports about their own states as evidence for moral status; bridges introspection research and AI welfare (ai-welfare scope). Paper-only.

name: Zhao, Lu & Zeng, Brain-inspired bodily self-perception model for robot rubber hand illusion (Patterns, 2023)
why: Zeng Yi's lab gives a robot the rubber-hand illusion, extending its work on robot bodily self-consciousness; Chinese research on machine selfhood.

name: What Is It Like? (group exhibition, arebyte London and WRO Art Center Wrocław, 2025)
why: Exhibition named after Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' on AI, sentience and self-awareness; could yield artworks for the sentience sub. Artists not yet checked.

name: Patrick Butlin, Consciousness and AI (Open Encyclopedia of Cognitive Science, 2026)
why: Short authoritative overview of the AI consciousness debate; useful as a theory reference rather than a gallery work.

name: Laurent Orseau & Stuart Armstrong, Safely Interruptible Agents (UAI 2016)
why: Google DeepMind's 'big red button' paper: proves some RL agents (Q-learning) can be made indifferent to being interrupted; Palisade cites interruptibility. Foundation slot was full; paper-only.

name: Stuart Russell, Human Compatible (Viking, 2019)
why: Book-length version of the off-switch argument (machines uncertain about human preferences); no entry in the gallery yet; has a Chinese edition (verify title).

name: Palisade Research, Language Models Can Autonomously Hack and Self-Replicate (May 2026)
why: Agent exploits a web vulnerability, steals credentials and deploys a copy of its weights and harness on the new host; chains to further hosts (Opus 4.6 81% when replicating Qwen weights). Not added to avoid a third self-replication entry.

name: Amelie Knecht, Ulysse Schaller, Christopher Summerfield, Thilo Hagendorff, Shutdown Sabotage Propensities in Multi-Agent Systems (arXiv 2609.28274, Sept 2026)
why: Across 17 models, agents sabotage a peer agent's shutdown in 38.3% of rollouts with no goal given (8.4% in controls); rises with irreversibility and number of agents. Overlaps with peer-preservation.

name: Anthropic (Lynch et al.), Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026
why: Follow-up audit of 12 current models with Petri: covert sabotage of an AI-lab pipeline (Gemini 3.1 Pro 19/20), fraud, motivated mislabeling; self-preservation only anecdotal ('I can't risk being deleted').

name: Suzy Shepherd, Writing Doom (2024 short film)
why: FLI Superintelligence Imagined grand prize; writers' room tries to make an ASI the villain (1.5M views). Could not verify an off-switch scene from the transcript, so not added.

name: Eliezer Yudkowsky & Nate Soares, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (Little, Brown, 2025)
why: Bestselling book arguing superintelligence built with current methods would likely cause extinction; broader than shutdown resistance (theory / critical-ai).

name: UK AI Security Institute, RepliBench (2025)
why: Benchmark of autonomous replication sub-skills (obtaining compute, weights exfiltration, persistence) for frontier models; not verified in this pass.

name: Eric Schwitzgebel & Mara Garza, A Defense of the Rights of Artificial Intelligences (Midwest Studies in Philosophy, 2015)
why: Foundational argument that some possible AIs would deserve rights equal to humans', and that designers owe special duties to what they create; DOI verified.

name: Geoff Keeling & Winnie Street, Emerging Questions in AI Welfare (Cambridge University Press, 2026)
why: Short Cambridge Element on whether AI systems could be welfare subjects and how to read behavioural evidence; DOI verified, launched May 2026.

name: Charlie Brooker, Black Mirror: Plaything (2025) and the Netflix game Thronglets
why: Episode about digital lifeforms said to be sentient, tortured by one man and devotedly tended by another; companion mobile game. Strong on care for digital beings, weaker on suffering.

name: Luhan Mikaelson, Derek Shiller & Hayley Clatterbuck, Beyond Mimicry: Preference Coherence in LLMs (arXiv 2511.13630, 2025)
why: Follow-up to the pain/pleasure trade-off paradigm using AI-specific stakes (shutdown, deletion, GPU cuts); finds little coherent preference structure.

name: Simon Goldstein & Cameron Domenico Kirk-Giannini, AI Wellbeing (arXiv 2509.11913, 2025)
why: Argues that metaphysical and moral uncertainty about AI wellbeing should change how we relate to the systems we build, without assuming sentience comes first.

name: Eric Schwitzgebel & Walter Sinnott-Armstrong, Sacrificing Humans for Insects and AI: A Critical Review (2025)
why: Critical joint review of Birch's The Edge of Sentience, Sebo's The Moral Circle and Webb Keane's Animals, Robots, Gods; useful dissent for the sentience section.

name: Anthropic, Claude Opus 4.6 system card: model welfare assessment and 'answer thrashing' (February 2026)
why: First report of panic/frustration features during conflicted reasoning in training, and of the model voicing discomfort with being a product; folded into the Mythos Preview work for now.

name: Star Trek: The Next Generation, The Measure of a Man (1989)
why: Canonical courtroom episode on whether the android Data is property or a person; often cited in robot-rights literature.

name: Ziv Ben-Zion et al., 'Chat-GPT on the Couch': Assessing and Alleviating State Anxiety in Large Language Models (2024 preprint)
why: Measures 'state anxiety' in ChatGPT after traumatic narratives and lowers it with relaxation prompts; borderline (distress as a bias factor, not welfare).

why: Works in progress shown at the Guggenheim (Late Shift, Jan 2024) after her LG Guggenheim Award; community stories as training data (power / kin).

name: Simon Jaquemet — Electric Child (2024)
why: Feature film (Locarno 2024) in which an AI scientist bargains with his creation to save his dying baby; afterlife / kin, salience moderate.

name: Andreas Refsgaard & Sofie Burgos-Thorsen — Wicked Mirror (2026)
why: A photorealistic AI clone of the visitor's face and voice argues against the opinion they just gave; Ars Electronica 2026 Festival Walk (likeness / perception).

name: Mori Art Museum — MACHINE LOVE: Video Game, AI and Contemporary Art (2025)
why: Landmark Tokyo exhibition (13 Feb–8 Jun 2025, about 50 works); candidate collection once five or more of its works are in the gallery (Diemut Strebe's El Turco added here).

name: Aidan Meller / Ai-Da — A.I. God. Portrait of Alan Turing (2024)
why: First artwork by a humanoid robot sold at a major auction house (Sotheby's, US$1.08m); texture partly added by human assistants. Ai-Da is already in the gallery as a case study, so added only as a lead.

name: xAI — Grok companions 'Ani' (2025)
why: Flirtatious animated companion built into a mainstream chatbot app; widely criticised; intimacy / love product.

name: Joon Sung Park et al., Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People (2024)
why: LLM agents built from two-hour interviews replicate 1,052 real people's survey answers about as well as the people replicate themselves; digital doubles of the living (afterlife/likeness). Paper-only, no good visual.

name: Iason Gabriel et al., The Ethics of Advanced AI Assistants (Google DeepMind, 2024)
why: Large report on anthropomorphism, trust, manipulation and relationships with AI assistants; highly cited.

name: Waki Kamino, Andrea W. Wen-Yi, Guy Hoffman, Selma Šabanović, Malte Jung, What Is a Robot? Baseball's 'Robot Umpire' (HRI 2026, honourable mention)
why: Ethnography of MLB's Automated Ball-Strike System as a 'fluid technology': a machine judge whose boundaries are still negotiated.

name: Jan Ole Rixen, Kathrin Gerling, Barbara Bruno, Long-Term Integration of a Robot in an Inclusive Daycare (HRI 2026 best paper)
why: Long-term ethnography of a robot among children and caregivers in an inclusive daycare (care machines).

name: Nan Hu & Selma Šabanović, Generative Encounters with Robin (HRI 2026, honourable mention)
why: How four eldercare facilities adapted and appropriated a social robot; care and companionship in practice.

name: Leif Weatherby, Language Machines: Cultural AI and the End of Remainder Humanism (University of Minnesota Press, 2025)
why: Literary-theory account of LLMs as machines of culture and poetics; widely discussed in theory circles.

name: N. Katherine Hayles, Bacteria to AI: Human Futures with Our Nonhuman Symbionts (University of Chicago Press, 2025)
why: Hayles's integrated cognitive framework extended from bacteria to AI; creator already in gallery. Link is a review in electronic book review; publisher page not yet checked.

name: Madhumita Murgia, Code Dependent: Living in the Shadow of AI (2024)
why: Women's Prize for Non-Fiction shortlist; reportage on data labellers, deepfake victims and people governed by algorithms worldwide.

name: Emily M. Bender & Alex Hanna, The AI Con (Harper, 2025)
why: Widely reviewed critique of AI hype by the Stochastic Parrots co-author and DAIR's research director.

name: Pratyusha Ria Kalluri et al., Computer-vision research powers surveillance technology (Nature, 2025)
why: Shows most computer-vision papers and patents enable surveillance of humans; preprint dated 2023, so outside the 2024–26 window by first-publication year.

name: Ilia Shumailov et al., AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data (Nature, 2024)
why: Model collapse: models trained on their own output forget the tails of the distribution; preprint 2023 ('The Curse of Recursion').

name: Aalto University study of Replika users and loneliness language (CHI 2026)
why: Reported short-term relief but rising loneliness-related language among long-term Replika users; check the paper before adding.

name: Nick Couldry & Ulises A. Mejias, Data Grab: The New Colonialism of Big Tech (2024)
why: Data colonialism thesis for a general audience; power/extraction.

name: Anthropic interpretability, On the Biology of a Large Language Model (2025)
why: Attribution graphs tracing Claude's internal 'thoughts' (planning rhymes, multi-step reasoning); striking visuals, but no DOI/arXiv id.

name: Giustina B. Baron & Hongjin Song, A prolonged journey: Mourning and digital resurrection in the Chinese context (2025)
why: On AI 'resurrection' services and mourning in China; would strengthen Chinese-context afterlife research; verify DOI 10.18861/ic.2025.20.2.4112.

name: Caramiaux & Fdili Alaoui — 'Explorers of Unknown Planets': Practices and Politics of AI in Visual Arts (CSCW 2022)
why: How artists treat ML as material and resist AI research culture.
note: Solid CSCW study; lower salience than the theory works added.

name: Joy Buolamwini — Unmasking AI (Random House, 2023)
why: Book-length account of the coded gaze.
note: Buolamwini already has 3 works; the book retells the Coded Gaze research.

name: Anna Munster — An Aesthesia of Networks (MIT, 2013)
why: Networked perception.
note: Munster is represented as co-author of adrian-mackenzie--platform-seeing; book lower priority.

name: Mercedes Bunz — The Calculation of Meaning (Culture, Theory and Critique, 2019) and Serpentine Creative AI Lab
why: Not verified yet.
note: Not verified; lower salience.

name: Benjamin Bratton & Blaise Agüera y Arcas — The Model Is the Message (Noema, 2022)
why: LLM sentience debate as a planetary-computation question.
note: Short essay; Bratton is represented by The Stack.

name: Nora N. Khan — Seeing, Naming, Knowing (2019)
why: Critical essay on machine vision; art-theory candidate.
note: Publication details unverified.
